{{Short description|Theorem in general relativity}}
{{general relativity|expanded=theorems}}
The '''Goldberg–Sachs theorem''' is a result in Einstein's theory of [[general relativity]] about vacuum solutions of the [[Einstein field equations]] relating the existence of a certain type of [[congruence (general relativity)|congruence]] with algebraic properties of the [[Weyl tensor]].

More precisely, the theorem states that ''a [[Vacuum solution (general relativity)|vacuum solution]] of the Einstein field equations will admit a shear-free null geodesic congruence if and only if the Weyl tensor is [[Petrov classification#The classification theorem|algebraically special]].''

The theorem is often used when searching for algebraically special vacuum solutions.

==Shear-Free Rays==
A ray is a family of geodesic light-like curves. That is tangent vector field <math>l^a</math> is null and geodesic: <math>l_a l^a = 0</math> and <math>l^b \nabla_b l^a = 0</math>. At each point, there is a (nonunique) 2D spatial slice of the tangent space orthogonal to <math>l^a</math>. It is spanned by a complex null vector <math>m^a</math> and its complex conjugate <math>\bar{m}^a</math>. If the metric is time positive, then the metric projected on the slice is <math>\tilde{g}^{ab} = -m^a \bar{m}^b - \bar{m}^a m^b</math>. Goldberg and Sachs considered the projection of the gradient on this slice.

<math> A^{ab} = \tilde{g}^{ap} \tilde{g}^{bq} \nabla_p l_q = z \bar{m}^a m^b + \bar{z} m^a \bar{m}^b + \bar{\sigma} m^a m^b + \sigma \bar{m}^a\bar{m}^b.</math>

A ray is shear-free if <math>\sigma=0</math>. Intuitively, this means a small shadow cast by the ray will preserve its shape. The shadow may rotate and grow/shrink, but it will not be distorted.

==The Theorem==
''A vacuum metric, <math>R_{ab}=0</math>, is algebraically special if and only if it contains a shear-free null geodesic congruence; the tangent vector obeys <math>k_{[a}C_{b]ijc}k^ik^j=0</math>.''<ref name="original_paper">{{cite journal |last1=Goldberg |first1=J. N. |authorlink1=Joshua N. Goldberg |last2=Sachs |first2=R. K. |authorlink2=Rainer K. Sachs |title=A theorem on Petrov types (republished January 2009)|journal=General Relativity and Gravitation |date=1962 |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=433–444 |doi=10.1007/s10714-008-0722-5 |s2cid=122155922 }}; originally published in Acta Phys. Pol. '''22''', 13–23 (1962).</ref>

This is the theorem originally stated by Goldberg and Sachs. While they stated it in terms of tangent vectors and the [[Weyl tensor]], the proof is much simpler in terms of spinors. The [[Newman-Penrose field equations]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Penrose |first1=Roger |title=Spinors and space-time Volume 1 two-spinor calculus and relativistic fields |date=1984 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0-521-24527-3}}</ref> give a natural framework for investigating [[Petrov classification|Petrov classifications]], since instead of proving <math>k_{[a}C_{b]ijc}k^ik^j=0</math>, one can just prove <math>\Psi_0 = \Psi_1 = 0</math>. For these proofs, assume we have a spin frame with <math>o^A</math> having its flagpole aligned with the shear-free ray <math>l^a</math>.

'''Proof that a shear-free ray implies algebraic specialty''': If a ray is geodesic and shear-free, then <math>\varepsilon + \bar{\varepsilon} = \kappa=  \sigma = 0</math>. A complex rotation <math>o^A \rightarrow e^{i\theta} o^A</math> does not affect <math>l^a</math> and can set <math>\varepsilon=0</math> to simplify calculations. The first useful NP equation is <math>D \sigma - \delta \kappa = 0</math>, which immediately gives <math>\Psi_0=0</math>.

To show that <math> \Psi_1=0</math>, apply the commutator <math>\delta D - D \delta</math> to it. The Bianchi identity gives the needed formulae: <math> D \Psi_1 = 4 \rho \Psi_1</math> and <math> \delta \Psi_1 = (2 \beta +4 \tau) \Psi_1</math>.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Newman |first1=Ezra |s2cid=121898444 |title=An Approach to Gravitational Radiation by a Method of Spin Coefficients |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |date=1962 |volume=3 |issue=3 |page=566|doi=10.1063/1.1724257 |bibcode=1962JMP.....3..566N }}</ref> Working through the algebra of this commutator will show <math>\Psi_1^2 = 0</math>, which completes this part of the proof.

'''Proof that algebraic specialty implies a shear-free ray''': Suppose <math>o_A</math> is a degenerate factor of <math>\Psi_{ABCD}</math>. While this degeneracy could be n-fold (n=2,3,4) and the proof will be functionally the same, take it to be a 2-fold degeneracy. Then the projection <math>o^Bo^Co^D \Psi_{ABCD} = 0</math>. The Bianchi identity in a vacuum spacetime is <math>\nabla^{AA'}\Psi_{ABCD} = 0</math>, so applying a derivative to the projection will give <math>o_A o_B \nabla^{AA'}o^B =0</math>, which is equivalent to <math>\kappa = \sigma = 0.</math> The congruence is therefore shear-free and almost geodesic: <math>D l_a = (\varepsilon+\bar{\varepsilon}) l_a</math>. A suitable rescaling of <math> o^A </math> exists which will make this congruence geodesic, and thus a shear-free ray. The shear of a vector field is invariant under rescaling, so it will remain shear-free.

==Importance and Examples==
In Petrov type D spacetimes, there are two algebraic degeneracies. By the Goldberg-Sachs theorem there are then two shear-free rays which point along these degenerate directions. Since the Newman-Penrose equations are written in a basis with two real null vectors, there is a natural basis which simplifies the field equations. Examples of such vacuum spacetimes are the [[Schwarzschild metric]] and the [[Kerr metric]], which describes a nonrotating and a rotating black hole, respectively. It is precisely this algebraic simplification which makes solving for the Kerr metric possible by hand.

In the Schwarzschild case with time-symmetric coordinates, the two shear-free rays are
<br /><math> l^\mu\partial_\mu = \pm\left(1 - \frac{2M}{r} \right)^{-1} \partial_t + \partial_r.</math>

Under the coordinate transformation <math>(t,r,\theta,\varphi) \rightarrow (t\mp r^* , r,\theta, \varphi)</math> where <math>r^*</math> is the [[Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates|tortoise coordinate]], this simplifies to <math>l^\mu \partial_\mu = \partial_r</math>.

==Linearised gravity==
It has been shown by Dain and Moreschi<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Dain|first=Sergio|title=The Goldberg-Sachs theorem in linearized gravity|journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics|year=2000|volume=41|issue=9|pages=6296–6299|doi=10.1063/1.1288249|arxiv=gr-qc/0203057|bibcode=2000JMP....41.6296D |s2cid=39619544 }}</ref> that a corresponding theorem will not hold in [[linearized gravity]], that is, given a solution of the [[linearised Einstein field equations]] admitting a shear-free null congruence, then this solution need not be algebraically special.
